papers.title: Service Design-Driven Formation of Dynamic Capabilities for International Service Innovation: A Case Study of a Chinese NEV Firm
papers.abstract: Amidst the acceleration of internationalization, service innovation has emerged as a critical pathway for New Energy Vehicle (NEV) firms to attain sustainable growth. Adopting a dynamic capability view, this study examines how service design drives the formation of dynamic capabilities in the context of international service innovation. Through a case study of a leading Chinese NEV firm, the research identifies how designerly practices enable the sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring of capabilities needed for service innovation across markets. The findings reveal a service design-driven capability formation model that integrates user research, prototyping, and iterative co-creation to bridge local market needs with global service architecture.

papers.title: Investigating the microfoundation of dynamic managerial and organizational capabilities for business model innovation: a mediated-moderated model of artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: In rapidly evolving digital environments, organizations must develop dynamic capabilities to drive business model innovation (BMI). This study examines how dynamic managerial capabilities (DMCs), including managerial cognition, social capital, and human capital, interact with dynamic organizational capabilities (DOCs) to facilitate BMI. Using a mediated-moderated model, we investigate the mediating role of DOCs between DMCs and BMI, and the moderating role of artificial intelligence (AI) capability. Structural equation modeling analysis of survey data from firms undergoing digital transformation reveals that AI capability significantly amplifies the mediating effect of DOCs, acting as a catalyst for BMI. Environmental uncertainty strengthens the AI-DMC-BMI relationship.

papers.title: Dropping Pebbles: The Ripple Effect of Designerly Co-creation in Steering Sustainability Transitions in Hospitals
papers.abstract: Steering sustainability transitions in complex organizations, such as hospitals, may benefit from iterative, situated, and participatory experimentation. Co-creation holds particular promise in this regard, as it can catalyze change by involving diverse stakeholders. Yet, the mechanisms through which designerly co-creation contributes to sustainability transitions in healthcare settings remain underexplored. Through multiple case studies in hospital settings, this paper develops the Pebble Effect model, illustrating how small-scale design interventions create ripple effects across organizational layers, enabling emergent and sustained sustainability transitions. Key factors include the cultivation of internal change agents and the design of post-intervention autonomy.

papers.title: Driving Public Service Innovation Through Internal Ecosystem Development: Reconfiguring the Internal Management and Service System of Nanhai Bus Station
papers.abstract: As public sectors worldwide increasingly adopt design-driven approaches to address complex public service and management challenges, existing research predominantly focuses on citizen-facing experiences and service touchpoints. This paper presents a case study of the Nanhai Bus Station in China, demonstrating how design-driven ecosystem development can reconfigure internal management and service systems. The research reveals how internal ecosystem restructuring through designerly methods enables public service organizations to innovate beyond the front-stage, transforming back-office operations, inter-departmental collaboration, and value delivery architecture.

papers.title: Emergent Innovation in Systemic Programme Design: Retrospective Reflections on the Development of a Student-Centred Masters in Systems Thinking
papers.abstract: Our theory of education, based on a systemic understanding of the subjective and intersubjective construction of knowledge, is that students are motivated to study what is most meaningful to them. This paper presents retrospective reflections on the development of a student-centred Masters programme in Systems Thinking, tracing how emergent innovation occurred through systemic programme design principles. The authors identify key patterns of emergent innovation including iterative co-design with stakeholders, adaptive curriculum structures, and the cultivation of learning communities that transcend institutional boundaries. The study contributes to understanding how systemic design principles can enable innovation in educational and organizational programme development.

papers.title: Trends and Challenges in Service Design Methods
papers.journal: International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: Service design has become increasingly important in addressing the growing complexity of contemporary socio-technical service ecosystems shaped by digital transformation, artificial intelligence, and multi-channel customer interactions. As service environments become more dynamic and user-centred, organisations require more integrated, sustainable, and participatory approaches to service innovation. However, existing service design methods remain fragmented, often focusing on isolated service requirements, specific stages of development, or single disciplinary perspectives. Consequently, there is limited understanding of how service design methodologies collectively evolve to address complex and interdisciplinary service environments. This study examines the trends and challenges of service design methods through a thematic analysis of 63 service design methods using the Zettelkasten (slip-box) organisation technique. The methods were integrated into a Sunburst Chart to visualise hierarchical relationships, process stages, and key methodological elements. Based on this analysis, a comprehensive service design process framework was developed to evaluate the evolution of service design methodologies. The findings indicate that service design methods are evolving towards more integrated, systemic, and holistic approaches. Nevertheless, major challenges remain in sustaining user engagement, eliciting implicit user requirements, supporting interdisciplinary co-creation, developing modular multi-interface systems, enabling automated value co-creation, and ensuring sustainability through iterative evaluation and long-term value-in-use. This study contributes a comprehensive analytical framework that supports the development of adaptive, sustainable, and human-centred service design methodologies for increasingly complex service environments.

papers.title: A Perceived Value Framework for Automotive Design Innovation: Rethinking Strategic Transition of Incumbent OEMs in the Post-ICE Era
papers.abstract: As the industry moves beyond the internal combustion engine, incumbent original equipment manufacturers (incumbent OEMs) need a systematic, experience perception-centred way to evaluate design. We introduce a Perceived Value Framework for Automotive Design Innovation that integrates functional, emotional, symbolic, and social value dimensions. The framework addresses the strategic design transition challenge facing incumbents navigating the post-ICE transformation, providing a structured approach to rethink product-service integration, brand positioning, and user experience design in the context of electrification and digital mobility services.

papers.title: Capturing the impact of co-creation in circular transitions: A comparative analysis of evaluation frameworks and models
papers.abstract: While participatory design approaches such as co-creation and co-design are increasingly used to develop circular solutions, there are limited contributions on assessing their impact. This paper systematically reviews existing evaluation frameworks and models to capture the impact of co-creation in circular transitions. Through comparative analysis, we identify key dimensions including process quality, outcome sustainability, stakeholder empowerment, and systemic change potential. The paper proposes an integrated evaluation model that addresses the temporal, spatial, and social complexity of co-creation impact in circular economy contexts, offering practical guidance for designers and researchers.

papers.title: From Greener growth to sufficiency: Modeling alternative global sustainability pathways
papers.abstract: This study quantifies two contrasting global sustainability scenarios—FST1: Greener Growth and FST5: Sufficiency Economies—using the MORDRED model. While both pursue high decarbonization without speculative technologies, they differ fundamentally in their assumptions about economic growth, consumption patterns, and social organization. The Greener Growth pathway relies on technological efficiency and green investment, while the Sufficiency pathway requires structural changes in production-consumption systems and social norms. Results show that Sufficiency scenarios achieve deeper sustainability outcomes but require more fundamental sociotechnical transitions. The study provides quantitative foundations for long-term sustainability strategy and policy design.
